How I work

Actions over stated intentions. Three habits do most of the work.

Triangulate

Interviews tell me what people believe. Session replays show what they do. Analytics tell me how often. A finding counts when all three agree.

Size the problem

Every qualitative insight gets a number attached before it reaches a roadmap, so teams argue about priority instead of about whether the problem is real.

Stay past the handoff

I follow findings into the A/B test and read the sessions behind the result. That's where misreads get caught, and where the next question comes from.

Transactional flow · Self-initiated

Why our most valuable travellers converted the worst

Families attached more extras than any other segment — and abandoned more often than any other segment. Nobody could explain the gap. This is how I closed it.

Role
Lead UX Researcher
Timeline
2 months
Team
1 researcher, 1 designer, 2 PMs, Director of Product
~€2M Projected annual net revenue from the two A/B tests that followed, B2C and B2B2C. The work became a prioritised roadmap item and a headline result in a leadership review.

In short

Problem
Families converted ~7 percentage points below solo travellers, while producing the highest expected revenue per booking. The funnel data showed the gap but not the cause.
What I did
Sized the gap in Mixpanel, then ran 5 parent interviews, comparative testing against Booking.com and 20 session replays in FullStory — and built prototypes of both flows to test head to head with 22 participants.
What I found
The passenger page and form were organised around passengers, not tasks. That forced parents to repeat the same decisions person by person — cognitive repetition that built fatigue and made them lose track of who was insured.
What happened
Group-level insurance went to A/B test in two markets. The task-centric passenger step became the declared product direction.

The question nobody could answer

I started this on my own initiative. Segmenting the booking funnel showed something uncomfortable: families — the segment attaching the most extras and generating the most revenue per booking — converted significantly worse than solo and group travellers.

The funnel told us where people left. It couldn't tell us why, and no one on the team had a working theory. Two questions framed the work: why do families convert worse than everyone else, and what is actually getting in their way?

How I approached it

Four methods, each chosen to answer something the previous one couldn't.

1 · Data exploration, to size the problem before touching it

I started quantitative on purpose. Interviewing first risks chasing whatever the first parent complains about. Segmenting the funnel in Mixpanel by trip type, country, language, currency, device and traveller type told me the gap was real, where it sat, and how much it was worth — so the qualitative work had a target.

2 · Interviews with parents, to understand the decision

Five parents aged 35–50 travelling with children. Booking for a family isn't one decision repeated, it's a set of trade-offs made on behalf of other people. I needed the mental model before I could judge whether our flow matched it.

3 · Unmoderated comparative testing, to separate our problems from the category's

Some friction is inherent to booking a flight for four people. Two groups booked the same trip on Kiwi.com and Booking.com in opposite orders, so order effects cancelled out and I could tell which problems were ours. Unmoderated so nobody performed for a facilitator.

4 · Session replay, to check what people actually did

Interviews and tests are artificial settings. 20 FullStory recordings of real families booking let me verify whether the behaviours I'd seen in testing showed up in production — and how often.

5 · Prototypes of both flows, tested head to head

Diagnosis isn't proof that your answer is better. I built two interactive prototypes myself with AI: a task-centric version of the fix, and a passenger-centric one replicating the flow that was live in production, as the control. Testing two working flows rather than a concept meant participants reacted to the experience, not to a description of it.

Two rounds, for two different questions. First, 12 participants split between the flows, to measure time and satisfaction without one flow contaminating the other. Then 10 participants through both, counterbalanced by starting order, to get a direct preference that order effects couldn't explain.

What I found

Funnel analysis

The segment worth the most converted the worst

Families converted roughly 7 percentage points below solo and group travellers, while generating the highest expected revenue per booking of any segment. The gap was concentrated on exactly the bookings the business most wanted to win, which is what made it worth a month.

Interviews + usability testing + session replay

People think in tasks. The form thought in passengers.

The flow made you finish everything for one person before starting the next: details, baggage, insurance, repeated passenger by passenger. For a family of four that's the same decision made four times. The usability testing showed the repetition and the cognitive load; the replays showed it in production.

Insurance was the clearest case. Parents treat it as one decision for the family. Treating it as a per-passenger step meant they lost track of who was covered, and some family members ended up uninsured without anyone noticing.

Comparative prototype testing

The task-centric flow won on every measure

8 of 10 participants preferred it, and preference held regardless of which flow they saw first. It was 1.21 minutes faster on average, and rated a consistent 5 — "very easy" — against ratings scattered between 2 and 5 for the live flow.

8/10preferred task-centric
-1.21minon task time
5/5ease, vs 4 and scattered

Error handling was the sharpest difference. The task-centric flow surfaced a missing field in real time, next to the traveller it belonged to. The live flow only raised it after Continue, leaving people to scroll back and hunt for it — a pattern FullStory confirmed in production, where 2 in 10 people entering passenger names hit that alert.

The two who preferred the live flow wanted per-passenger control: "fills out separately for each individual — gives me even more control." That minority is why the final design kept a per-traveller option rather than removing it.

Interviews + session replay

Mandatory paid seating reads as unfair, not as a fee

Some airlines require paid seating when travelling with children or infants. Participants didn't object to paying — they objected to paying without being allowed to choose the seat. Session data showed it as a clear drop-off point, and competitors defer it to post-booking.

From insight to decision

Findings don't ship. I'd set up a weekly research touchpoint with the PMs and the Director of Product, so this landed in a conversation that already existed rather than as a deck nobody asked for.

I framed the three recommendations by how much they cost to build, so the team could say yes to something immediately instead of debating the whole redesign:

  1. Restructure the passenger form around tasks, not passengers: details, then baggage, then insurance, for everyone at once. The full fix.
  2. Bundle insurance at family level so it can be chosen for the whole group in one action. The quick win — most of the value, a fraction of the work, and the one that shipped first.
  3. Omit or defer mandatory paid seating to post-booking, as competitors do, rather than charging for a seat the traveller can't pick.

I also took it beyond my own team. I presented the findings and the prototype results in a cross-functional product forum with senior leadership, so the case was argued where the roadmap is actually set.

The PM cited the research as the basis for the initiative, which went on to become a prioritised roadmap item and a headline result in a leadership review.

What shipped

Group-level insurance went to A/B test in B2C and then B2B2C. Travellers are now insured for the whole group in a single action, with per-passenger control still available for the families who want it.

I stayed on past the handoff. During the experiment I analysed sessions on the per-traveller toggle and found most people opened it to check their selection rather than to change it — only one in nine chose different plans per passenger. That settled an open design debate in favour of keeping a single group-level control.

The task-centric passenger step became the declared product direction, and the remaining components are scheduled for release.

Limits, and what I'd do differently

  • In B2B2C, the revenue metrics never reached significance before the variant was promoted. Conversion did.
  • The qualitative samples were small — 22 participants across two rounds, 20 replays. Enough to find the pattern and show a clear preference, not enough to size the effect, which is why every finding above is backed by funnel data as well.

Transactional flow · Self-initiated

The button that wasn't a button

Users were tapping the price box to continue, then wondering why nothing happened. Six sessions showed me the behaviour; production data told me how much it was costing.

Role
Lead UX Researcher
Timeline
1 month
Team
1 researcher, 2 designers, 2 engineers, 1 PM
+6.8% payment success rate Expected gross profit per visitor trended up around 10%, a directional signal that did not reach significance.

In short

Problem
Most users leave the booking flow on the first page, and payment is one of the biggest drop-offs. Exit surveys gave reasons like "just browsing" — nothing a team could act on.
What I did
Ran moderated think-aloud testing on people's own real trips, then checked whether what I saw happened in production, and sized it with behavioural analytics.
What I found
The price box read as the primary button, and it overlapped the real one while scrolling. 4% of users opened it and closed it instantly — a misclick, not a price check.
What happened
The redesign went to an A/B test on metasearch traffic. Payment success rate rose 6.8%, a significant result, and expected gross profit per visitor trended up around 10%.

Why the survey wasn't enough

Most users exit the booking flow on the first page, and payment is one of the biggest drop-offs. The team's goal was simple — convert more of the people who already decided to buy a ticket — but nobody knew what was stopping them.

We had exit-survey answers: not ready to buy, just browsing, couldn't complete the payment. Useful for sizing intent, useless for finding usability problems, because people can't report friction they never noticed. If the interface was getting in the way, the survey would never say so. That's what sent me looking at behaviour instead.

How I approached it

Three methods, each answering what the previous one couldn't.

1 · Moderated think-aloud testing on real trips

Six participants, each booking a trip they were actually planning rather than a scenario I invented, so the decisions and the hesitation were real. I chose moderated over unmoderated here because I needed to probe: ask what they expected to happen, and why they did what they just did. That's where the price-box behaviour first appeared.

2 · Session replay, to test it outside the lab

Six people in a facilitated session isn't evidence of a production problem. I built a FullStory segment of users who clicked the price box and watched what they did immediately before and after. The behaviour showed up in 7 of 20 recordings.

3 · Behavioural analytics, to tell accident from intent

A click on the price box could be someone checking the fare. To separate the two, I measured the time between opening it, closing it and continuing. An instant open-and-close followed by progression isn't price-checking — it's a misfire. That gave the pattern a number instead of an impression.

What I found

Moderated testing

People read the price box as the primary button

Participants tapped the price box to move forward, then tapped it again when nothing happened. It sits at the bottom of the screen, it's the most prominent element there, and while scrolling it overlapped the real call to action — so the thing that looked like the way forward was also covering the way forward.

"What happened? How do I continue now?"

Session replay + behavioural analytics

4% of users opened the price box and shut it immediately

They opened it, closed it within moments and carried on. Nobody checking a fare behaves that way. The short interaction and the immediate progression both point to the same thing: they meant to continue, not to look at pricing.

The same confusion was worse at payment, where at certain scroll positions the price box sat on top of the pay button — not slowing people down but stopping them from paying at all.

From insight to decision

The finding was easy to dismiss as a minor visual issue, so I framed the two recommendations around what each would cost to build and what it would protect — the payment step first, since that one was blocking transactions outright.

  1. Stop the layers overlapping, so the price box and the primary button never occupy the same visual plane. The urgent fix, especially at payment.
  2. Redesign the price box and strengthen the visual hierarchy of the primary call to action, so Continue and Pay read as the obvious next step.

Both were accepted and built with the designers and engineers on the team, and the redesign went to an A/B test before rolling out.

What shipped

The redesign made the price box look less like a call to action and unified it with the rest of the step. In the A/B test on metasearch traffic, payment success rose 6.8%, the primary metric's statistically significant result. Expected gross profit per visitor trended up around 10%, a trend rather than a confirmed effect.

It's a small adjustment at a decision point where a lot of money passes through. That's the argument I'd make again: friction doesn't have to be dramatic to be expensive.

Limits, and what I'd do differently

  • Six participants is enough to spot a pattern, not to size it. That's exactly why the finding only reached the team once production data backed it, and I'd keep that sequence.
  • The test changed more than one thing at once — the price box looking less like a button, and unifying it with the rest of the step — so the uplift can't be split between them.
  • The gross profit gain is a trend, not a result. Its interval crosses zero.
  • The 4% figure is inferred from timing, not stated intent. It's a strong signal, but it's a behavioural proxy, and I'd say so rather than call it a measured error rate.

Fintech · Checkout

People pressed Pay before choosing how to pay

A survey told us people "couldn't complete the payment". It didn't say why. Finding out meant watching what they actually did at checkout — and then arguing for it with a team that wasn't mine.

Role
Lead UX Researcher
Timeline
3 months
Team
1 researcher, 1 designer, the Fintech team and its leadership
2 recommendations shipped Default payment-method preselection and method-specific pay buttons went live in the new Payment Library, the rollout that reported an 8% lift in successful payments. Further findings were prioritised by the team.

In short

Problem
Checkout was fragmented across the booking and post-booking flows. The exit survey's top answer was "I couldn't complete the payment" — a symptom, not a cause.
What I did
Analysed 20 session replays of people who dropped at payment, sized the patterns with Mixpanel and FullStory, and presented the findings to the Fintech team.
What I found
14% of Pay clicks happened with no method selected, and those sessions converted ~25% worse. Third-party payment flows also failed for a meaningful share of clicks.
What happened
Two recommendations shipped in the Payment Library, the rollout that reported an 8% lift in successful payments. Further findings were prioritised by the team.

A symptom, not a cause

The payment experience was split between the booking flow and the post-booking flow, inconsistent across platforms, and the team was deciding how to unify it. The strongest evidence we had was an exit survey I'd run in 2023, where the most common reason for abandoning was "I couldn't complete the payment".

That answer is a dead end on its own. It tells you people failed, not what failed. And the kind of friction that stops a payment — a button that doesn't respond as expected, a redirect that silently fails — is precisely the kind people can't articulate afterwards. So the question became behavioural: what do people who drop at payment actually do, just before and just after?

How I approached it

Three methods, moving from what people said to what they did to how often.

1 · The exit survey, as a starting point rather than an answer

I'd run it myself in 2023, and I went back to it to narrow the search. It pointed at payment specifically rather than checkout in general, which is what justified spending the next phase on the payment step alone instead of the whole flow.

2 · Session replay of people who dropped at payment

20 FullStory recordings of real payment droppers. Watching them was the only way to see the sequence: what they clicked, what happened next, and how they tried to recover. The two main findings both came from here, and neither was something a survey could have surfaced.

3 · Behavioural analytics, to size what I'd seen

A pattern in 20 sessions is a hypothesis. I used Mixpanel and FullStory across the user base to measure how often each friction occurred and how much each one cost in conversion, so the team could prioritise by impact rather than by whichever story was most vivid.

What I found

Session replay + behavioural analytics

14% of Pay clicks happened with no payment method selected

People pressed Pay before choosing how to pay, hit an alert, and then had to work out what had gone wrong. Those sessions converted around 25% worse than the rest.

The recovery behaviour was the telling part. Users went back into the booking flow, hesitated at payment, and repeatedly deselected and reselected methods after the alert fired. They weren't ignoring the requirement; the interface never made it legible in the first place.

Session replay + behavioural analytics

Third-party payments broke quietly

Some third-party payment flows failed silently, with redirects that never reached the provider. From the user's side none of this reads as a technical failure — it reads as "this doesn't work", and they leave.

The pay button also didn't change when the method changed, so nothing told people what pressing it would actually do.

From insight to decision

This was someone else's roadmap. The Fintech team owned the checkout, and I had no authority over what they built — only evidence and the chance to present it well.

I presented the findings in a workshop with the Fintech team. Framing each friction with its cost in conversion mattered more than any single recommendation, because it let the team argue about priority instead of about whether the problem was real.

  1. Preselect a payment method so the step can never start in a state that fails.
  2. Make the pay button reflect the selected method, so what will happen next is legible before pressing it.
  3. Let returning users save PayPal and Google accounts, cutting the redirects where most third-party failures happened.

The first two shipped in the new Payment Library. The third was prioritised for later.

What shipped

The payment step now opens with a method already selected, and the button names the method it will use — Pay with Google Pay rather than a generic Pay. The extra confirmation layer that used to sit between the user and the provider is gone from the booking flow.

Rolled out to post-booking, the Payment Library reported an 8% lift in successful payments. Two of the recommendations inside it were mine.

Before — the two-step detour

Limits, and what I'd do differently

  • I can't claim the Payment Library's business result. It was built by the Fintech team and bundled several changes — saved cards, mixed payments, a new interface — that didn't come from my research. What I can point to is which recommendations shipped.
  • Preselection shipped with a different rule than I proposed. I recommended the last method used; what launched was a fixed order. The problem it solves is the one I identified, but the solution isn't the one I designed.
